title: The unnoticed term
bodyMd:
Contract law often supplies default terms that apply when the parties say nothing about a particular issue. Such terms are sometimes defended as approximations of what most parties would have chosen. If nearly everyone prefers a certain delivery rule, making it the default saves them the trouble of writing it repeatedly. On this account, the ideal default is the most popular imagined bargain. The parties remain free to write a different term, which is why a default differs from a mandatory prohibition. Nevertheless, the freedom to depart does not make the initial rule inconsequential. Writing alternatives takes time, and some parties assume that standard terms need no attention. A default can consequently shape agreements even when nobody actively endorses it. Its justification must take account of that inertia rather than imagine that every unchanged term has been deliberately selected after comparison with all possible alternatives.

That defense leaves out a second possible purpose. A default can be designed to encourage the party with better information to reveal it. Suppose a customer knows that a routine delivery delay would cause that customer an unusually large loss, but has not disclosed this vulnerability to the carrier. A rule that limits compensation unless the special risk is declared can give the customer a reason to disclose it. The parties can then decide whether extra precautions are worth their cost. The default is not necessarily the term they would prefer after full discussion; it helps induce the discussion.

This information-forcing strategy has limits. A party may fail to disclose not because the default creates the wrong incentive, but because the party never reads or understands it. Requiring disclosure through an obscure rule can punish inattention without producing useful information. The strategy also assumes that the informed party can communicate the fact at reasonable cost and that the other party can respond meaningfully.

Default design therefore requires more than counting preferences. Designers must ask what parties know, what they notice, and what behavior a rule is likely to produce before anyone opts out. A majority-preferred default may minimize drafting costs in one setting, while a conspicuous disclosure-triggering default may improve decisions in another. Calling either approach universally superior would overlook the very transaction conditions that make it work.
